questions.q: Who holds the power in a democracy?
questions.a: The people hold the power and use it to elect representatives. A wrong answer suggests the student thinks power resides only with the leader, failing to recognize the role of the voter.

questions.q: How does a leader usually come to power in a monarchy?
questions.a: Power is usually inherited through birth, meaning it stays within the royal family. A wrong answer suggests the student confuses monarchy with democracy (voting) or dictatorship (force).

questions.q: If a person forces their way into power and refuses to listen to the citizens, what type of government is this?
questions.a: This is a dictatorship. Steps: 1. Identify the lack of public choice. 2. Identify the use of force or absolute control. 3. Match these traits to the definition of a dictatorship. A wrong answer indicates an inability to distinguish between "forceful control" and "elected authority."

questions.q: Compare a democracy and a monarchy: what is the main difference in how the leader changes?
questions.a: In a democracy, the leader changes through elections; in a monarchy, the leader changes through family succession. A wrong answer reveals a failure to differentiate between "public choice" and "birthright."

questions.q: Is it possible for a country to be both a democracy and a monarchy?
questions.a: Yes, some countries have a monarch as a symbolic head, but the actual power to make laws rests with elected representatives (a constitutional monarchy). A wrong answer suggests a rigid, overly simplistic view that doesn't account for modern political systems.

questions.q: If you were to design a new government for a school club, which type would you choose and why?
questions.a: A good answer chooses a system and justifies it using the concept of power (e.g., "I choose democracy so everyone has a voice"). A poor answer fails to connect the choice to the source of power.
